headline_marked: I tested Samsung's Auto Blocker and Google's Advanced Protection; [[you'll want both on]]
headline: I tested Samsung's Auto Blocker and Google's Advanced Protection; you'll want both on
summary: A deep dive reveals Samsung's Auto Blocker and Google's Advanced Protection barely overlap, providing comprehensive security when used together on Galaxy devices.
details: Samsung's Auto Blocker and Google's Advanced Protection, both available on Galaxy devices, initially seem redundant. However, testing reveals they offer distinct security layers that complement each other, providing more comprehensive protection when enabled simultaneously.

Auto Blocker, a Samsung feature, prevents app installation from unauthorized sources, blocks USB commands, stops malware images in messaging apps, and halts USB software updates. Its standard level is on by default and can re-enable itself 30 minutes after being temporarily turned off.

Google's Advanced Protection, introduced with Android 16 and brought to Galaxy phones with One UI 8, is designed for users at higher risk of targeted attacks. It offers both device and Google account protection and is not enabled by default.

The primary overlap between the two features is blocking sideloading and 2G networks. Advanced Protection further extends its reach by blocking updates to apps that were sideloaded before the feature was activated.

Beyond this, Auto Blocker secures the physical and Samsung-specific aspects of your phone, including dial codes and Samsung apps. Advanced Protection, conversely, focuses on Google's ecosystem, covering Chrome, Google Messages, and Play Protect.

Enabling both features does come with trade-offs, such as restricting app installations to the Play Store or Galaxy Store, and limiting USB commands or certain dial codes. However, these minor inconveniences are outweighed by the significantly enhanced security.

Neither feature provides complete coverage on its own. Together, they create a robust security posture, leaving very few gaps in protection for your Galaxy device. For even more privacy, users can leverage the Secure Folder.

headline_marked: [[Ad-tech company Discover-Tech was a delivery system for 'mercenary spyware']] via zero-click malware
headline: Ad-tech company Discover-Tech was a delivery system for 'mercenary spyware' via zero-click malware
summary: Citizen Lab's "Exposing AdFection" report reveals how major ad-tech firms, including Google and Facebook, were exploited by Discover-Tech to serve zero-click malware to targeted individuals.
details: Citizen Lab's "Exposing AdFection" report concludes that the ad-tech system is so insecure it allowed total compromise of digital devices. It reveals how major ad-tech companies were hijacked by a "mercenary spyware" firm.
This firm used the ad system to locate targeted individuals and serve "zero-click malware." This malware took over computers and phones without any user action required.
Tech giants like Google and Facebook amassed detailed surveillance dossiers and assigned unique identifiers to users. This allowed "advertisers" to serve arbitrary code based on these identifiers.
Israeli company Discover-Tech, masquerading as an ad-tech firm, sold totalitarian governments the ability to target individuals. They served "malicious ads" containing "no-click, zero-day" attacks.

These attacks exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities, compromising devices simply by loading a webpage or opening an app. Al Jazeera workers were among the targets, attacked with malware from Candiru.
Discover-Tech was "certified" as a safe supplier by Google, Yandex, Microsoft, Beeswax (Comcast), and IAB. This certification gave it access to over four billion ad-auctions.
This access allowed Discover-Tech to collect user identities, check them against target lists, and launch attacks. The company has ties to other Israeli spyware firms, including NSO Group.

The incident highlights the monumental insecurity of the ad-tech industry, whose insufficient vetting and auditing expose users to targeted attacks. Companies claim prudence, but have hosted cyber-mercenaries for years.
The only way to avoid these attacks is to block ads. While easy in browsers, modifying apps to block ads is often illegal, leaving app users vulnerable.
